rules.statement: An entity shall account for a contract with a customer only when all five criteria are met: the parties have approved the contract and are committed to perform, each party's rights are identifiable, payment terms are identifiable, the contract has commercial substance, and it is probable the entity will collect the consideration it is entitled to.

Collectibility of substantially all the consideration must be probable (a higher US-GAAP threshold, ~75%, vs IFRS 15's 'probable' = more likely than not, ~50%) before revenue can be recognised on a contract.

At contract inception an entity shall identify as performance obligations each promise to transfer a distinct good or service, or a series of substantially the same distinct goods or services with the same pattern of transfer.
A good or service is distinct if the customer can benefit from it on its own or with readily available resources, and the promise is separately identifiable from other promises in the contract.

The transaction price is the amount of consideration an entity expects to be entitled to in exchange for transferring promised goods or services, excluding amounts collected on behalf of third parties (e.g. sales taxes).

Variable consideration is included in the transaction price only to the extent it is probable that a significant reversal of cumulative revenue will not occur when the uncertainty is subsequently resolved (the constraint).

An entity shall adjust the promised consideration for the time value of money when the timing of payments provides the customer or the entity with a significant financing benefit; a practical expedient exempts contracts where the period between transfer and payment is one year or less.
An entity shall allocate the transaction price to each performance obligation in proportion to its relative standalone selling price.
Revenue is recognised when (or as) the entity satisfies a performance obligation by transferring control of the promised good or service to the customer.

A performance obligation is satisfied over time if any one of three criteria is met: the customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits, the entity's performance creates/enhances a customer-controlled asset, or the asset has no alternative use and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for performance to date.

If a performance obligation is not satisfied over time, it is satisfied at a point in time when the customer obtains control, indicated by present right to payment, legal title, physical possession, risks and rewards of ownership, and customer acceptance.

When either party has performed, the contract shall be presented as a contract asset or contract liability depending on the relationship between the entity's performance and the customer's payment; an unconditional right to consideration is presented as a receivable.

The incremental costs of obtaining a contract shall be capitalised as an asset if the entity expects to recover them; a practical expedient allows expensing when the amortisation period would be one year or less.

At the commencement date a lessee shall recognise a right-of-use asset and a lease liability for all leases (other than short-term leases it elects to exempt); unlike IFRS 16's single-model approach, US GAAP retains a dual lessee classification.

The lease liability is measured at the present value of lease payments not yet paid, discounted using the rate implicit in the lease or, if not readily determinable, the lessee's incremental borrowing rate.
The right-of-use asset is initially measured as the lease liability plus prepaid lease payments and initial direct costs, less lease incentives received.

A lessee classifies a lease as a finance lease if any one of five criteria is met: transfer of ownership, a purchase option reasonably certain to be exercised, lease term for the major part of the asset's remaining economic life, present value of payments substantially all of the asset's fair value, or the asset is so specialised it has no alternative use to the lessor; otherwise it is an operating lease.
For a finance lease the lessee recognises interest on the lease liability and amortisation of the right-of-use asset separately, producing a front-loaded total expense pattern.

For an operating lease the lessee recognises a single lease cost on a straight-line basis over the lease term, unlike the finance-lease split — a key US-GAAP divergence from IFRS 16 which treats nearly all leases as finance-type.

A lessee may elect, by class of underlying asset, not to recognise a right-of-use asset and lease liability for short-term leases (term of 12 months or less with no reasonably certain purchase option), recognising lease payments on a straight-line basis instead.

A lessor classifies each lease as sales-type, direct financing, or operating; sales-type when any finance-lease criterion is met, direct financing when collection is probable and a third-party residual guarantee covers the remaining payments, otherwise operating.

A lessee shall remeasure the lease liability when there is a change in the lease term, the assessment of a purchase option, the amounts probable of being owed under a residual value guarantee, or an index/rate-driven change in future payments.

Inventory is initially measured at cost, comprising all expenditures (direct and indirect, including a systematic allocation of fixed and variable production overheads) incurred to bring it to its existing condition and location.
Permissible cost-flow assumptions include FIFO, weighted-average, and LIFO; LIFO is permitted under US GAAP but is prohibited under IFRS (IAS 2) — a material US-vs-IFRS difference.
Inventory measured using any method other than LIFO or the retail inventory method (e.g. FIFO or average cost) shall be measured at the lower of cost and net realizable value.

Inventory measured using LIFO or the retail inventory method is measured at the lower of cost or market, where market is current replacement cost subject to a NRV ceiling and a NRV-less-normal-profit floor.
Net realizable value is the estimated selling price in the ordinary course of business less reasonably predictable costs of completion, disposal, and transportation.

A write-down of inventory to the lower of cost and NRV (or market) creates a new cost basis that is not subsequently reversed for later recoveries in value — unlike IAS 2, which requires reversal of prior write-downs.

The lower-of-cost-and-NRV test may be applied on an item-by-item basis, by major category, or at another level that most clearly reflects periodic income, provided losses are not inappropriately deferred.

Property, plant and equipment is recorded at historical cost, including the purchase price and all costs necessary to bring the asset to working condition for its intended use; US GAAP does not permit the IFRS revaluation model.
The depreciable cost of PP&E shall be allocated over its estimated useful life in a systematic and rational manner.
A long-lived asset (asset group) held and used shall be tested for recoverability whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate that its carrying amount may not be recoverable.

Carrying amount is not recoverable if it exceeds the sum of the undiscounted cash flows expected from the asset's use and eventual disposition (an impairment indicator); this undiscounted step is a US-GAAP feature absent from IAS 36, which uses a single discounted recoverable-amount test.

If carrying amount is not recoverable, an impairment loss is measured as the excess of carrying amount over fair value; the loss establishes a new cost basis and shall not be reversed in future periods.
A long-lived asset classified as held for sale shall be measured at the lower of its carrying amount and fair value less costs to sell, and depreciation ceases while it is held for sale.

Goodwill shall not be amortised but tested for impairment at least annually at the reporting-unit level and more frequently if a triggering event indicates it is more likely than not impaired (consistent with IAS 36).
A goodwill impairment loss is measured as the amount by which a reporting unit's carrying amount exceeds its fair value, limited to the carrying amount of goodwill allocated to that unit.

A private company or not-for-profit may elect the accounting alternative to amortise goodwill on a straight-line basis over 10 years (or less if shorter is more appropriate) and test for impairment only upon a triggering event.

An intangible asset with a finite useful life shall be amortised over that life and reviewed for impairment under ASC 360; an intangible with an indefinite life is not amortised but tested for impairment at least annually.
An indefinite-lived intangible asset is impaired if its carrying amount exceeds its fair value, and the impairment loss equals that excess.

Costs incurred during the application-development stage of internal-use software shall be capitalised; costs in the preliminary-project and post-implementation/operation stages are expensed as incurred.

Capitalised internal-use software costs shall be amortised on a straight-line basis over the software's estimated useful life unless another systematic and rational basis is more representative of its use.

Research and development costs shall be charged to expense when incurred; US GAAP does not permit capitalisation of development costs, unlike IAS 38 which capitalises development costs meeting six criteria.

Materials, equipment, and facilities acquired or constructed for R&D that have alternative future uses are capitalised and depreciated; if there is no alternative future use, their cost is expensed as R&D when incurred.
A deferred tax liability or asset shall be recognised for the estimated future tax effects attributable to temporary differences and carryforwards using the asset-and-liability method.

Deferred tax assets and liabilities shall be measured using the enacted tax rate expected to apply in the periods the temporary differences are expected to reverse; only enacted rates may be used (not substantively-enacted rates as IAS 12 permits).
A valuation allowance shall be recognised to reduce a deferred tax asset to the amount that is more likely than not (>50%) to be realised, based on all available positive and negative evidence.

The benefit of an uncertain tax position is recognised only if it is more likely than not to be sustained on examination based on its technical merits, assuming the taxing authority has full knowledge.
A recognised uncertain tax position is measured as the largest amount of benefit that is greater than 50% likely to be realised upon settlement with the taxing authority.
Deferred tax assets and liabilities shall be classified as noncurrent on a classified balance sheet, and those for each tax-paying jurisdiction shall be netted into a single noncurrent amount.
A statement of cash flows shall classify cash receipts and payments into operating, investing, and financing activities.
Operating activities include all transactions and events that are not investing or financing activities, generally the cash effects of transactions entering into the determination of net income.
Investing activities include making and collecting loans and acquiring/disposing of debt or equity instruments and property, plant and equipment.

Financing activities include obtaining resources from and returning them to owners, and borrowing and repaying amounts borrowed; unlike IAS 7, US GAAP prescribes fixed classification for interest, dividends, and tax cash flows.

Cash flows from investing and financing activities shall generally be reported gross rather than net, except where qualifying for net presentation (e.g. quick turnover, large amounts, short maturities).
The statement of cash flows shall explain the change during the period in the total of cash, cash equivalents, and amounts generally described as restricted cash or restricted cash equivalents.
A change in accounting principle shall be reported through retrospective application to all prior periods presented, unless it is impracticable to determine the period-specific or cumulative effects.
A change in an accounting estimate shall be accounted for prospectively in the period of change and future periods if the change affects both; prior periods are not restated.

An error in previously issued financial statements shall be corrected by restating the prior-period financial statements affected (a restatement), with the cumulative effect adjusting the opening balance of retained earnings of the earliest period presented.

When retrospective application is impracticable, the new principle is applied to the carrying amounts of assets and liabilities as of the beginning of the earliest period to which it can be applied, with a corresponding adjustment to opening retained earnings.

An estimated loss from a loss contingency shall be accrued by a charge to income if it is probable that a liability has been incurred at the balance-sheet date and the amount can be reasonably estimated; both conditions must be met.

When a loss is probable and only a range can be estimated with no single amount being the best estimate, the minimum amount in the range shall be accrued (IAS 37 instead uses the midpoint of the range).

A loss contingency that is at least reasonably possible but not accrued (because it is not probable or not estimable) shall be disclosed, including the nature of the contingency and an estimate of the possible loss or range, or a statement that such an estimate cannot be made.
A gain contingency shall not be recognised in income before it is realised; recognition prior to realisation would risk recognising revenue that may never materialise.

Fair value is the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date (an exit price), aligned with IFRS 13.

Fair value measurements shall maximise the use of observable inputs and minimise unobservable inputs, categorised in a three-level hierarchy that gives highest priority to Level 1 inputs and lowest to Level 3 inputs.
Level 1 inputs are quoted prices (unadjusted) in active markets for identical assets or liabilities that the entity can access at the measurement date.

Level 2 inputs are inputs other than quoted prices included in Level 1 that are observable for the asset or liability, either directly or indirectly (e.g. quoted prices for similar items, interest rates, yield curves).

Level 3 inputs are unobservable inputs for the asset or liability, used when relevant observable inputs are not available and reflecting the entity's own assumptions about market-participant assumptions.
A fair value measurement of a non-financial asset shall consider its highest and best use by market participants, whether that use is in combination with other assets or on a standalone basis.

Management shall evaluate, each annual and interim reporting period, whether conditions raise substantial doubt about the entity's ability to continue as a going concern within one year after the financial statements are issued.

A classified balance sheet shall separate current assets and current liabilities from noncurrent items, with current items being those expected to be realised or settled within one year or the operating cycle, whichever is longer.
Current assets comprise cash and other assets reasonably expected to be realised in cash, sold, or consumed within one year or the normal operating cycle, whichever is longer.
Current liabilities are obligations whose liquidation is reasonably expected to require the use of current assets or the creation of other current liabilities within one year or the operating cycle.

Assets and liabilities shall not be offset on the balance sheet unless a right of setoff exists (the parties owe determinable amounts, the entity intends to set off, and the right is legally enforceable).
An entity shall report comprehensive income — net income plus other comprehensive income — either in a single continuous statement or in two consecutive statements.

Other comprehensive income comprises revenues, expenses, gains, and losses that under GAAP are excluded from net income, such as certain foreign-currency translation, pension, and available-for-sale debt-security adjustments.

Reclassification adjustments shall be presented to avoid double-counting items reported in net income in the current period that were also reported in other comprehensive income in the current or prior periods.

Interest cost shall be capitalised as part of the cost of an asset that requires a period of time to get ready for its intended use (a qualifying asset), measured by applying the capitalisation rate to the average accumulated expenditures.

An allowance for credit losses on financial assets measured at amortised cost shall reflect the current estimate of all expected credit losses over the asset's contractual life (the CECL model), recognised at initial recognition.

US GAAP has no general onerous-contract provision for revenue contracts equivalent to IFRS 15.34/IAS 37; loss provisions arise only under specific topics (e.g. construction-type contracts), a notable US-vs-IFRS difference.

A right-of-use asset shall be tested for impairment in accordance with ASC 360, and after an impairment the lessee amortises the remaining ROU asset over the shorter of its remaining useful life and lease term.
